points.description: Purpose: both are broadcast methods that reduce/avoid duplicate packets compared with plain flooding (more efficient broadcasting).
points.partial_credit: Says only that they are used for broadcasting, without mentioning fewer duplicates/efficiency.

points.description: Reverse Path Forwarding: a node forwards a broadcast packet (to all neighbours except the incoming one) only if it arrived from the neighbour that the node's unicast routing table would use to reach the source, i.e. the packet came along the best path; otherwise it is dropped.
points.partial_credit: Mentions checking the routing table / best path to the source but is vague about forwarding or dropping.

points.description: Reverse Path Broadcast: works like RPF, but nodes learn (e.g. by observing unicast traffic) which links belong to a spanning tree/best paths, and forward only on those tree edges (not back on the incoming link), reducing duplicates further.
points.partial_credit: Says it is like RPF with an extra restriction to some edges/tree, but without how this is learned or used.

rubric.notes: Full marks for stating the purpose (fewer duplicates than flooding) and giving the main idea of how each method works, in any wording. Give part marks for vague but on-track answers, e.g. RPF uses the routing table to check the best path to the source, and RPB restricts forwarding to spanning-tree links. Give no marks for answers unrelated to broadcasting or duplicate reduction. Wrong extra remarks do not cost marks unless they contradict the central ideas.
